name: Beta9
summary: The open-source engine behind Beam’s cloud: decorate a Python function and it runs as an autoscaling GPU endpoint, task queue or sandbox, on Beam or on your own Kubernetes cluster.
intro: With Beta9 you add a decorator to a Python function, such as `@endpoint`, `@task_queue` or `@function`, and give it an image, CPU, memory and optionally a GPU. The platform builds the container, runs it, and scales the number of containers with the work waiting (for example, 30 queued tasks per container, up to five containers), down to zero when idle. A `Sandbox` is the same machinery driven from code: an isolated container you start, run commands or LLM-generated code in, snapshot and fork.

Underneath is a Go control plane (a gateway and a scheduler) and workers that run on Kubernetes. Self-hosting means installing its Helm chart on a cluster such as EKS, with CPU and GPU worker nodes, a container registry, and persistent PostgreSQL, Redis and S3-compatible storage. Workers can run each container with plain runc, inside gVisor, or as a Cloud Hypervisor microVM. Beam says a custom runtime, image caching and memory snapshots let containers start in under a second; that is the vendor’s figure, and big model weights still have to load.

Beta9 is what Beam’s hosted product runs on. Beam Cloud adds a managed workspace, dashboard, billing and hosted services, which a self-hosted install doesn’t get automatically; the SDK is the same apart from the package name (`beta9` instead of `beam`). The code is open source under the AGPL-3.0. It is young: the repository started in November 2023, its gateway and worker are still versioned 0.1.x with new tags almost daily, and most commits come from Beam’s own small team.
strengths: One decorator turns a function into an autoscaling GPU endpoint, task queue, scheduled job or sandbox, with scale to zero by default
Built for heavy AI containers: image caching, memory snapshots and checkpoint restore to cut cold starts
Choice of isolation per worker: runc containers, gVisor, or Cloud Hypervisor microVMs for untrusted code
The same code runs on Beam’s hosted cloud or on a cluster you control
limits: AGPL-3.0: if you modify it and let others use it over a network, you must offer them your changed source
Early-stage: components are still 0.1.x, change almost daily, and depend on a small team at one company
Self-hosting is a real platform to run (Kubernetes, GPU nodes, registry, ingress, PostgreSQL, Redis, object storage) and lacks some Beam Cloud features
Python-first: the decorator model lives in the Python SDK; the TypeScript SDK covers sandboxes and calling deployed endpoints

story: Luke Lombardi and Eli Mernit, college roommates, spent years at hackathons and built a serverless framework to ship web apps quickly. When they started working with machine learning, they found nothing comparable for deploying models, so they founded Beam in 2021 to build it. The company went through Y Combinator’s Winter 2022 batch.

Beam’s pitch was serverless for AI workloads, where container images are large, GPUs are expensive and cold starts hurt. Rather than run on Lambda or a stock Kubernetes setup, they wrote their own container runtime and distributed storage layer, used gVisor for isolation, and added memory snapshots and GPU checkpoint restore.

On November 15, 2023 the runtime appeared on GitHub as Beta9 under the AGPL-3.0, and Beam began presenting itself as an open-source, self-hostable alternative to Modal. It has since grown sandboxes for AI agents and a microVM runtime, while staying on pre-1.0 version numbers.

choices.choice: Python decorators instead of YAML and Dockerfiles
choices.why: The founders wanted to ship ML products without managing servers, Dockerfiles or security groups, so the resources and scaling rules sit next to the function they apply to.

choices.choice: A custom container runtime and storage layer
choices.why: AI images with model weights are large, and pulling them on every cold start is slow. Caching and snapshotting at the runtime level is how Beam keeps start-up times down.
Sandboxes run code written by users or generated by LLMs, so containers sharing a host kernel need a stronger boundary than plain runc.

choices.choice: Open-source core under a hosted product
choices.why: Beam positions itself against platforms that lock customers in: the same code can move between Beam’s cloud and a self-hosted cluster.
